No, not in this case. The assumption of unit cost arithmetic is simply not physically realizable. It's probably easier to understand the integer case: numbers take bits to store and represent. In a typical computer, you would store numbers as either 32 or 64 bits, where 32 bits could store a number up to about 4 billion (or a signed number between -2 and +2 billion). If you want to store and multiply numbers larger than that, they take up more space and they require more work on the part of the processor, and fundamentally, more energy - adding two 128 bit numbers takes twice the work as adding two 64 bit numbers.

The same applies to the precision of floating point numbers. What Ben is arguing is happening in this case is the AI has found a way to hide work by moving it into operations that, in one (unrealistic) model of computation, are assumed to cost the same regardless of how large or precise the numbers are. I think the conclusion that CGI made sense to die then but not now is probably correct, but for a different reason.

The main reason CGI died in large part is because it wasn't fast enough. Not the only reason for sure, but this is the general consensus. Spawning cgi children was slow, etc. Solutions were built to do in-process CGI, or separate CGI daemons. This even happened per-language with in-process CGI support for Perl, etc.

In the end, as people wanted more speed, they moved away from CGI to various other ways of doing things (client side, etc).

This aspect probably no longer makes sense - i'd be shocked if you couldn't make CGI "fast enough" these days without anywhere near as many hoops. To the degree hoops are necessary, they are probably saner to implement.

That doesn't mean folks should move back to CGI of course - but as i said, it is probably accurate that the main reason it died probably does not hold up anymore.

during transcription, nothing is actually "playing" the file in the way a human would to listen to it. the audio is stored as a sequence of bytes representing the amplitude of the physical sound waves over time (the recording device measures, or "samples", the amount that its microphone is vibrating and records that amount, some tens of thousands of times per second) with some metadata and compression applied so that other software knows how to interpret the bytes correctly. this can be given to an audio program to convert the bytes back to physical sound waves using your speakers, but it's just bytes at the end of the day, so any software that can read bytes out of the file can do so at whatever speed it wants, regardless of how long the actual recording is.

so you have a file containing bytes representing the sound wave, and you have existing recordings (read: sound waves represented as sequences of bytes) of people speaking in different languages and contests, and you can feed all those existing recordings into a model along with corresponding transcriptions, and you can get a model out which can identify patterns in recordings of people speaking to then go backwards and see a pattern of sound waves and correctly associate it with a specific token, no need to play anything back. pauses, stutters, etc. are themselves patterns of sound waves that can be identified and worked around to identify just the meaningful parts of speech.

in principle, you could probably learn to do this too, by sitting down for hundreds of hours meticulously starting at waveforms, and this is, very roughly, what signal analysts do: look at waveforms and try to identify patterns. ai just leverages this principle to turn mundane speech into text.

Eg. the mentioned commit says that pinephone SoC MIPI-PLL is unstable at 432 MHz, yet it does not acknowledge what that driving the panel at 16% faster clock may result into at all, from 16% higher power drain due to every userspace app having to render at 70 Hz, to stutter of video playback or UI stutter in systems that don't derive all timing from the display (eg. if input is read at 60Hz and output is done at 70Hz this can really mess up the UI feel) to behavior on borderline panels.

Panel clocked at higher than expected frequency may not complete the required LCD dicharge process correctly/completely due to compressed time (and this error may accumulate over several power on/off cycles), because it works with different than expected timings to complete a fixed physical process. (partly speculating here - what I know for sure is that this issue that causes flickering accumulates over several power on/off cycles if poweroff is done wrongly)

In any case, for my kernel I prefer 60Hz and underlocked PLL (works on all my 5 pinephones) so I revert that 500 MHz PLL limit in my kernel and run the panel at specified frequency. I don't see any flicker issues on my devices other than during development/hard poweroffs, etc..

I created an Android app called HandyPC.

When working on a physical device, logs, configuration files, and text files are all on the device. Yet, when making corrections, I had to transfer them to my PC, make the corrections, and then transfer them back. I created HandyPC because I wondered why I had to transfer them outside when they were already there.

The core function is file management. You can navigate through files using Explorer, open them with a text editor, and perform search and replace, as well as check character encoding and line breaks. It also handles zip files. You can add tabs to increase the number of windows, and up to two panes can be arranged side-by-side.

For days when you need more advanced features, I've included SCP, SSH, terminal, and network diagnostics (ping, traceroute, port check, DNS, etc.) in the same app. You can also see what's connected via a USB-C wired LAN adapter.

It's built with React Native and Kotlin. It's free for the first two months after installation, and then a one-time purchase.

Technically, it's nothing new. I simply combined existing features into a single app for continuous use. I'd like to ask people who are doing the same round trip whether this is sufficient, or what they think is missing.
